procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 26.04.2014 of the High Court of Judicature at Bilaspur (CG) in Criminal Appeal No. 45 of 2003.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature at Bilaspur (CG) affirmed the conviction and sentence imposed by the Trial Court in Criminal Appeal No. 45 of 2003.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court dismissed the Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No. 5631 of 2018, thereby upholding the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court also noted that the victim's name was disclosed in the judgments of both the trial court and the High Court, which is inconsistent with Section 228-A of the IPC. The Court directed the Registry of the High Court to take steps to ensure compliance with Section 228-A by trial courts in the State.

directions: The Registry of the High Court is directed to place the record of the appeal in the High Court before the learned Judge for causing appropriate changes in the record including passing appropriate practice directions so that the trial courts in the State comply with the mandate and spirit of Section 228- A IPC.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence of the petitioner under Sections 376 and 342 of the IPC, as affirmed by the High Court, should be overturned.

facts: The petitioner was convicted by a trial court under Sections 376 (rape) and 342 (wrongful confinement) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
He was sentenced to seven years and one year, respectively.
The High Court affirmed the conviction and sentence by dismissing the petitioner's appeal.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the case and the prior judgments from the High Court and the trial court.
The Court stated that it did not see any reason to interfere with or "upset" the previous orders of conviction and sentence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, thereby upholding the petitioner's conviction and sentence as affirmed by the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the disclosure of the rape victim's identity in the judgments of the lower courts is inconsistent with the mandate and spirit of Section 228-A of the IPC.

facts: The victim of rape, who was a witness (PW-2), was named throughout the judgments of both the trial court and the High Court.
law: Section 228-A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) prohibits the disclosure of the identity of a victim of rape.
An explanation to Section 228-A provides an exception for judgments of a superior court.
The Supreme Court precedent in State of Punjab v. Ramdev Singh (2004) 1 SCC 421 establishes that courts should make every attempt not to disclose the victim's identity.
application: The Supreme Court observed that naming the victim in the lower court judgments was inconsistent with the mandate of Section 228-A of the IPC.
The Court acknowledged the exception for superior court judgments but emphasized that, nonetheless, all courts should strive to protect the victim's identity in line with the spirit of the law.
Citing its previous ruling in State of Punjab v. Ramdev Singh, the Court reinforced the principle of non-disclosure.

To rectify the error and prevent future occurrences, the Court directed the High Court's Registry to make appropriate changes to the record to anonymize the victim's identity and to issue practice directions for trial courts to ensure compliance with Section 228-A.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the disclosure of the rape victim's identity in the lower court judgments was inconsistent with the mandate and spirit of Section 228-A of the IPC. Despite an exception in the law, the Court held that the practice should be avoided and ordered the High Court to amend its records and issue guidelines to ensure future compliance by all courts in the state.

cases.case_name: State of Punjab v. Ramdev Singh
cases.principle: That every attempt should be made by all the courts not to disclose the identity of the victim in terms of Section 228-A IPC.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Every attempt should be made by all courts not to disclose the identity of the victim of a sexual offense, in accordance with Section 228-A of the Indian Penal Code.
obiter: While the explanation to Section 228-A of the Indian Penal Code makes an exception for the judgments of a superior court, the practice of naming a victim is inconsistent with the spirit of the law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found no reason to interfere with the petitioner's conviction and sentence as affirmed by the lower courts. However, it also found that the repeated disclosure of the rape victim's name in the judgments of the trial court and the High Court was inconsistent with the mandate and spirit of Section 228-A of the IPC, even though an exception exists for superior court judgments.
legal_tests_applied: Consistency with Section 228-A of the Indian Penal Code, which governs the disclosure of a rape victim's identity.
Adherence to the precedent set in State of Punjab v. Ramdev Singh (2004) 1 SCC 421, which mandates that courts should not disclose the identity of the victim.
why_appellant_lost: The court saw 'no reason to upset the orders of conviction and sentence' that had been affirmed by the High Court.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position to uphold the conviction was successful because the Supreme Court found no basis to interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts.
policy_considerations: Despite a technical exception in Section 228-A IPC for judgments of superior courts, the court reasoned that 'every attempt should be made by all the courts not to disclose the identity of the victim' in order to comply with the 'mandate and spirit' of the law.
